title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
R Graphics VS ggplot

R Graphicsggplot2



hist(exam_data$MATHS)











ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = 'black',
                 fill = 'grey') +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths scores")

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Bar chart: geom_bar()

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= RACE)) +
  geom_bar()

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Dot plot: geom_dotplot()
Width of dot corresponds to the bin width (or max width, depending on binning algorithm), and dots are stacked, with each dot representing one observation.

ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(dotsize = 0.5)














WarningBe careful



The y scale is not very useful and in fact is misleading. As such it is better to turn off y-axis using scale_y_continous().



ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth=2, dotsize = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)














Note



The difference in the first and the second code is the additional binwidth argument. The binwidth controls the binning. The dotsize is scaling the drawing of the dots. So just having binwidth argument means binning is controlled and ggplot automatically default the dot size to 1, as shown below. Having only the dotsize argument means ggplot bins according to its default but size of the dot is controlled as shown in the first code. And having both arguments means that ggplot have to follow the binning and size of the dot specified as shown in the second code.



ggplot(data = exam_data,
       aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = 2.5)

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Histograms: geom_histograms()
The code chunk below is an example to create a simple histogram by using values in MATHS field of exam_data

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram()

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Density: geom_density()
geom_density() computes and plots kernel density estimate, which is smoothed version of the histogram. Useful alternative to the histogram for continuous data that comes from an underlying smooth distribution.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_density()

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Boxplot: geom_boxplot()
geom_boxplot() displays continous value list. It visualises five summary statistics (the median, two hinges and two whiskers), and all “outlying” points individually.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot()








Notches are used in box plots to help visually assess whether medians of distributions differ. If the notches do not overlap, this is evidence that the medians are different.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE)








From this, it can be seen that the median is not the same.

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Violin plot: geom_violin()
geom_violin() creates violin plot which is a way to compare multiple data distributions. With ordinary density curves, it is difficult to compare more than just a few distributions because the lines visually interfere with each other. With a violin plot, it’s easier to compare several distributions since they’re placed side by side.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER)) +
  geom_violin()

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
Scatterplot: geom_point()

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point()

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
section: Modifying geometric object by changing geom()
text:
Modifying geometric object by changing geom()
Lets use histogram as an example. Bins argument is the number of bins. Fill argument is the shade of the histogram. Color is the outline color of the bars. So, the code below means that the number of bins is 20, with light blue shade outlined with black.

ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x= MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, color='black', fill='light blue')

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
section: Modifying geometric object by changing aes()
text:
Modifying geometric object by changing aes()
We could add a subgroup by using colour, fill, shape argument in aes().

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           colour = GENDER)) +
  geom_density()









ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           fill = GENDER)) +
  geom_histogram(bins=20, color='black')









ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS, 
           y = ENGLISH, 
           shape = GENDER)) +
  geom_point()














Note



Scatterplot can use shape and colour. Bar and histogram can use fill. Density can use colour. Dot plot can use shape, colour and fill. Alpha can also be used in aes() which controls the opacity.

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
geom objects can be combined
The code chunk below combine scatterplot and boxplot.

ggplot (data=exam_data,
        aes(y = MATHS, 
            x = GENDER)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(position='jitter', size = 0.5)














Note



Jitter is used for the position so that a random noise is given to very point, which can prevent overplotting where dots might overlap.

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
stat_summary() method
Below is a simple boxplot that is incomplete because the positions of the means are not shown.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER))+
  geom_boxplot()








Now add stat_summary() function and override default geom.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER))+
  geom_boxplot() +
  stat_summary(geom = 'point',
               fun = 'mean',
               colour = 'red',
               size = 4)

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
geom() method

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(y = MATHS, x = GENDER))+
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat = 'summary',
             fun = 'mean',
             colour = 'red',
             size = 4)

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
section: Adding best fit curve on scatterplot
text:
Adding best fit curve on scatterplot
Below is a scatterplot between Maths and English grades of students.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point()








The interpretability of this graph can be improved by adding a best fit curve. This is done using geom_smooth().

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(size = 0.5)








The default smoothing method used is loess. But this can be overridden as shown below.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5)

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
facet_wrap() function
facet_wrap() wraps a 1d sequence of panels into 2d. This is generally a better use of screen spae than facet_grid() because most displays are roughly rectangular.
The code chunk below plots a trellis plot using facet_wrap().

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_wrap(~ CLASS)








It is also possible to do a combination as shown in the code chunk below.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_wrap(~ CLASS + GENDER)

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
facet_grid() function
facet_grid() forms a matrix of panels defined by row and column facetting variables. It is most useful when you have two discrete variables, and all combinations of the variables exits in the data.
The code chink below plots a trellis plot using facet_grid().

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_grid(~ GENDER)








The graph plot the trellis plot through column. It is possible to change the orientation to rows instead.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_grid(rows = vars(GENDER))








Again it is possible to do a combination as shown in the code chunk below.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_grid(vars(CLASS), vars(GENDER))

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
coord_flip() function
By default, bar chart of ggplot2 is in vertical form.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar()








The code chunk below flips the horizontal bar chart into vertical bar chart by using coord_flip().

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = RACE)) +
  geom_bar() +
  coord_flip()

title: Hands-on Excercise 1 - Layered Grammar of Graphics: ggplot Methods
text:
coord_cartesian() function
The scatterplot below is slightly misleading because the y-axis and the x-axis range are not equal.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5)








Lets fix both the y-axis and x-axis range from 0-100. The code chunk below does that.

ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS, y = ENGLISH)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = lm,
              linewidth = 0.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0,100),
                  ylim = c(0,100))

title: Hands-on Exercise 2 - Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
For this exercise, besides tidyverse, four R packages will be used. They are:

ggrepel: provides geoms for ggplot2 to repel overlapping text labels
ggthemes: provides some extra themes, geoms, and scales for ggplot2
hrbrthemes: provides typography-centric thems and theme components for ggplot2
patchwork: for preparing composite figure created using ggplot2

The code chunk below will check if the packages needed are installed and load them into R environment.

pacman::p_load(ggrepel, patchwork, ggthemes,
               hrbrthemes, tidyverse)




The data file used is called Exam_data which consists of year end examination grades of a cohort of primary 3 students from a local school. It is in csv file format.

exam_data <- read_csv("Exam_data.csv")

title: Hands-on Exercise 2 - Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
ggtheme package
ggtheme provides ggplot2 themes that replicate the look fo plots by Edward Tufte, Stephen Few, Fivethirteight, The Economist, Stata, Excel and The Wall Street Journal among others.
The code below used The Exonomist theme.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths score") +
  theme_economist()














Tip



It has many themes and provides some extra geoms and scales for ggplot2. Consult this site to see the various options.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2 - Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
hrbrthemes packages
hrbrthemes package provides base theme that focuses on typograohic elements including where various lables are placed as well as the fonts that are used.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths score") +
  theme_ipsum()








The second goal centers around productivity for a production workflow where presenting something needs to be visually clean and readable to increase reader’s engagement. Consult this site to learn more.

ggplot(data=exam_data,
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, 
                 boundary = 100,
                 color = "grey25",
                 fill = "grey90") +
  ggtitle("Distribution of Maths score") +
  theme_ipsum(axis_title_size = 18,
              base_size = 15,
              grid = 'Y')














TipWhat can be learnt from the code chunk above?




axis_title_size: controls font size of the axis title
base_size: controls the size of axis label
grid: controls the lines in the graph, in this case remove the x-axis grid lines

title: Hands-on Exercise 2 - Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
patchwork methods
There are several extension function that support composite figure by combining several graphs such as grid.arrange() of gridExtra package and plot_grid() of cowplot package. This section will focus on an extension called patchwork which is specially designed for combining ggplot2 graphs into a single figure.
Patchwok package has a very simple syntax wherewe can create layouts super easily. Here’s the general syntax:

Two-column layout using the plus sign +
Subplot group ysing paranthesis ()
Two-row layout using division sign /
Plot beside each other using |

Examples:

Combine 2 ggplot graphscombine 3 ggplot graphs



p1 + p2











(p1 / p2) | p3

















Tip



Another way is to use wrap_plots() to directly plot all the graphs into one section. Use #| fig-width and #| fig-height to change the size or scale of the figure. This one uses 15 and 7 respectively.

wrap_plots(p1, p2, p3)










To learn more, refer to Plot Assembly. The site has information about adding a table or some text and how to place it to the left of the graph.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2 - Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
Creating composite figure with tag
In order to identify subplots in text, patchwork also provides auto-tagging capabilities as shown below.

((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'I')

title: Hands-on Exercise 2 - Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
text:
Creating figure with inser
It is also possible to insert one or more plots or graphic elements freely on top or below another plot using inset_element().

p3 + inset_element(p2, 
                   left = 0.02, 
                   bottom = 0.7, 
                   right = 0.5, 
                   top = 1,
                   align_to = 'full')














Note



align_to specifies where the element should be relative to. ‘panel’ is the default, ‘full’ is for the whole image, ‘plot’ is for the plot area of the main layer.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2 - Beyond ggplot2 Fundamentals
section: Creating composite figure using patchwork and ggtheme
text:
Creating composite figure using patchwork and ggtheme

patchwork <- ((p1 / p2) | p3) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "1")
patchwork & theme_economist(dkpanel=TRUE) 














Tip



It is not possible to add both ggtheme and hrbrtheme as both as solid themes so adding both would result on the last theme added. For example if the code was pathwork & theme_economist() & theme_ipsum() the output will have the ipsum theme and no economist theme.

text:
Exam_data.csv is used for this exercise. read_csv() is used to read the csv file and import Exam_data into R.

exam_data <- read_csv("data/Exam_data.csv")

title: Hands-on Exercise 3 - Interactive Data Visualisation
text:
Tooltip effect
The code chunk below is a typical code chunk to plot an interactive statistical graph by using ggiraph package.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = ID),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)

girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618
)











Note



Notice that the code chunk consists of two parts. First, an interactive version of ggplot object will be created. In this case, geom_dotplot_interactive() is used to create the basic graph. Next, girafe() of ggiraph will be used to create an interactive svg object to be displayed on an html page.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3 - Interactive Data Visualisation
text:
Displaying multiple information on tooltip
The content of the tooltip can be customized by including a list object as shown in the code chunk below.

exam_data$tooltip <- c(paste0(     
  "Name = ", exam_data$ID,         
  "\n Class = ", exam_data$CLASS)) 

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(tooltip = exam_data$tooltip), 
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 8,
  height_svg = 8*0.618
)





The first 3 lines in the code is create a column called tooltip in Exam_data which is filled with the combined text of ID and CLASS values. Now this will act as the label for each student. Then this field is then called in line 7 tooltip = exam_data(tooltip) so that when building the chart it will use the new tooltip column instead.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3 - Interactive Data Visualisation
text:
Customizing tooltip sytle
opts_tooltip() of ggiraph is used to customize tooltip rendering by add css declaration. Refer to the code chunk below.

tooltip_css <- "background-color:white; #<<
font-style:bold; color:black;" #<<

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(              
    aes(tooltip = ID),                   
    stackgroups = TRUE,                  
    binwidth = 1,                        
    method = "histodot") +               
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,               
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(                                  
  ggobj = p,                             
  width_svg = 6,                         
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(    #<<
    opts_tooltip(    #<<
      css = tooltip_css)) #<<

title: Hands-on Exercise 3 - Interactive Data Visualisation
text:
Displaying statistics on tooltip
Code chunk below shows an advanced way to customise tooltip. Int his example, a function is used to cimpute 90% confident interval of the mean. The derived statistics are then displayed in the tooltip.

tooltip <- function(y, ymax, accuracy = .01) {
  mean <- scales::number(y, accuracy = accuracy)
  sem <- scales::number(ymax - y, accuracy = accuracy)
  paste("Mean maths score:", mean, "+/-", sem)
}

gg_point <- ggplot(data=exam_data, aes(x = RACE)) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS, 
                   tooltip=after_stat(
                     tooltip(y, ymax))),
               fun.data = "mean_se",
               geom = GeomInteractiveCol,
               fill = "light blue") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = MATHS), 
               fun.data = mean_se,
               geom = "errorbar", width = 0.2, size = 0.2)

girafe(ggobj = gg_point,
       width_svg = 8,
       height_svg = 8*0.618)

title: Hands-on Exercise 3 - Interactive Data Visualisation
text:
Styling hover effect
The code chunk below will change the css code for the highlighting effect.

p <- ggplot(data=exam_data, 
       aes(x = MATHS)) +
  geom_dotplot_interactive(
    aes(data_id = CLASS),
    stackgroups = TRUE,
    binwidth = 1,
    method = "histodot") +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL,
                     breaks = NULL)
girafe(
  ggobj = p,
  width_svg = 6,
  height_svg = 6*0.618,
  options = list(
    opts_hover(css = "fill: #202020;"),
    opts_hover_inv(css = "opacity:0.2;")
  )
)











Note



The default css style is an orange fill. In this example, the css in opts_hover() would mean the data points that are hovered over will have a close to black fill. But the css style of other data points will have their opacity reduced to 0.2 as set in opts_hover_inv().

title: Hands-on Exercise 3 - Interactive Data Visualisation
text:
Linked brushing
It is possible to create interactive coordinated visalisations where selecting data points in one widget automatically highlights or filters the corresponding data in another widget. Brush here mean click or drag to select data points in one chart. So a linked brushing means that by dragging to select data points in one chart, the same data points are simultaneously highlighted in another chart or table.

CodeOutput plot



d <- highlight_key(exam_data) 
p <- ggplot(d, 
            aes(ENGLISH, 
                MATHS)) + 
  geom_point(size=1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim=c(0,100),
                  ylim=c(0,100))

gg <- highlight(ggplotly(p),        
                "plotly_selected")  

crosstalk::bscols(gg,               
                  DT::datatable(d), 
                  widths = 5)        







Note




highlight() is a function of plotly package. It sets a variety of optins for brushing multiple plots. These options are primarily designed for linking multuple ploly graphs, and may not behave as expected when linking plotly to another htmlwidget package via crosstalk. In some cases, other htmlwidgets will respect these options, such as persistent selection in leaflet.
bscols() is a helper function of crosstalk package It makes it easy to put HTML elements side by side. It can be called directly from the console but is especially designed to work in a R Markdown document. Warning: This will bring in all of Bootstrap!

title: Hands-on Exercise 3 Part 2 - Programming Animated Statistical Graphics with R
text: When creating animations, the plot does not actually move. Instead, many individual plots are built and then stitched together as movie frames, just like an old-school flip book or cartoon. Each frame is a different plot when conveying motion, which is buil using some relevant subset of the aggregate data. The subset drives the flow of the animation when stitched back together.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3 Part 2 - Programming Animated Statistical Graphics with R
text:
Importing data
In this hands-on exercise, the Data worksheet from GlobalPopulation Excel workbook will be used. The code chunk below is used to import the data from GlobalPopulation by using appropriate R package from tidyverse family.

col <- c("Country", "Continent")
globalPop <- read_xls("data/GlobalPopulation.xls",
                      sheet="Data") %>%
  mutate_each_(funs(factor(.)), col) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year))







NoteThings to learn from the code chunk above




read_xls() of readxl package is used to import the Excel worksheet
mutate_each_() of dplyr package is used to convert all character data type into factor
mutate of dplyr package is used to convert data values of Year field into integer



Unfortunately, mutate_each_() was deprecated in dplyr 0.7.0. and funs() was deprecated in dplyr 0.8.0. In view of this, we will re-write the code by using mutate_at() as shown in the code chunk below.

col <- c("Country", "Continent")
globalPop <- read_xls("data/GlobalPopulation.xls",
                      sheet="Data") %>%
  mutate_at(col, as.factor) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year))

across() is also another alternative that can be used to derive the same outputs.

col <- c("Country", "Continent")
globalPop <- read_xls("data/GlobalPopulation.xls",
                      sheet="Data") %>%
  mutate(across(col, as.factor)) %>%
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year))

Building a static population bubble plot
Below is a basic static bubble plot

ggplot(globalPop, aes(x = Old, y = Young, 
                      size = Population, 
                      colour = Country)) +

Building the animated bubble plot

ggplot(globalPop, aes(x = Old, y = Young, 
                      size = Population, 
                      colour = Country)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, 
             show.legend = FALSE) +

  scale_size(range = c(2, 12)) +

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 1 - Visualising Distribution
section: Plotting ridgeline graph using ggridges method
text:
Plotting ridgeline graph using ggridges method
There are several ways to plot ridgeline plot with R. In this section, you will learn how to plot ridgeline plot by using ggridges package.
ggridges package provides two main geom to plot gridgeline plots, they are geom_ridgeline() and geom_density_ridges(). The former takes height values directlly to draw the ridgelines, and the latter first estimates data densitites and then draws those using ridgelines.
The code chunk below uses geom_density_ridges().

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH, y = CLASS)) +
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01,
    bandwidth = 3.4,
    fill = lighten("#7097BB", .3),
    color = "white") +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, 
                   expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 1 - Visualising Distribution
section: Varying fill colors along the x-axis
text:
Varying fill colors along the x-axis
Sometimes we would like to have the area under a ridgeline not filled with a single solid color but rather with colors that vary in some form along the x-axis. This effect can be achieved by using either geom_ridgeline_gradient() or geom_density_ridges_gradient(). Both geoms work just like geom_ridgeline() and geom_density_ridges(), except that they allow for varying fill colors. However, they do not allows for alpha transparency in the fill. For technical reasons, we can can eave changing fill colors or transpoarency but not both.

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = stat(x))) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(
    scale = 3,
    rel_min_height = 0.01) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Score",
                      option = "C") +
  scale_x_continuous( name = "English grades", 
                      expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_y_discrete(name = NULL, 
                   expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 2.6))) +
  theme_ridges()

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 1 - Visualising Distribution
section: Mapping the probabilities directly onto color
text:
Mapping the probabilities directly onto color
Besides providing additional geom objects to support the need to plot ridgeline plot, ggridges package also provides a stat function called stat_density_ridges() that replaces stat_density() of ggplot.
The code chunk is plotted by mapping the probabilities calculated using stat(ecdf) which represent the empirical cumulative density function for the distribution of English score.

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH,
           y = CLASS,
           fill = 0.5 - abs(0.5-stat(ecdf)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Tail probability",
                       direction = -1) +
  theme_ridges()














Important



It is important to include argument calc_scdf = TRUE in stat_density_ridges().

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 1 - Visualising Distribution
text:
Ridgeline plots with quantile lines
By using geom_density_ridges_gradients(), we can colour the ridgeline plot by quantile, via the calculated stat(quantile) aesthetic as shown in the code chunk below.

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
                      quantiles = 4,
                      quantile_lines = TRUE) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Quartiles") +
  theme_ridges()








Instead of using number to define the quantiles, we can also specify quantiles by cut points such as 2.5% and 97.5% tails to color the ridgeline plot as shown in the figure below.

ggplot(exam,
       aes(x = ENGLISH, 
           y = CLASS, 
           fill = factor(stat(quantile)))) +
  stat_density_ridges(geom = "density_ridges_gradient",
                      calc_ecdf = TRUE, 
                      quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Probability",
    values = c("#FF0000A0", "#A0A0A0A0", "#0000FFA0"),
    labels = c("(0, 0.025]", "(0.025, 0.975]", "(0.975, 1]")
  ) +
  theme_ridges()

Plotting a half eye graph
Plot Half-eye graph using stat_halfeye() of ggdist package.

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE,

  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA)














TipThings to learn from code chunk



We remove the slab interval by setting .width = 0 and point_colour = NA.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 1 - Visualising Distribution
text:
Adding the boxplot with geom_boxplot()
Next, add second geometry layer using geom_boxplot() of ffplot. This produces a narrow boxplot. We reduce the width and adjust the opacity.

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA)

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 1 - Visualising Distribution
text:
Adding Dot Plots with stat_dots()
Next, add third geometry layer using stat_dors() of ggdist package. This produces a half-dotplot, which is similar to a histogram that indicates the number of samples in each bin. We select side = “left” to inidicate we want it on the left-hand side.

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 2)

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 1 - Visualising Distribution
text:
Finishing touch
Lastly, coord_flip() of ggplot package will be used to flip the raincloud chart horizontally to give it the raincloud appearance. At the same time, theme_economist() of ggthmes package is used to give the raincloud chart a professional publishing standard look.

ggplot(exam, 
       aes(x = RACE, 
           y = ENGLISH)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5,
               justification = -0.2,
               .width = 0,
               point_colour = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = .20,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_dots(side = "left", 
            justification = 1.2, 
            binwidth = .5,
            dotsize = 1.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_economist()

Unpacking the Bayes Factor
A Bayes factor is the ratio of the likelihood of one particular hypothesis to the likelihood of another. It can be interpreted as a measure of the strength of evidence in favor of one theory among two competing theories.
That’s because the Bayes factor gives us a way to evaluate the data in facor of a null hypothesis, and to use external information to do so. It tells us what the weight of the evidence is in favor of a given hypothesis.
When we are comparing two hypotheses, H1 (the alternative hypothesis) and H0 (the null hypothesis), the Bayes Factor is often written as B10. It can be defined mathematically as

The Schwarz criterion is one of the easiest ways to calculate rough approximation of the Bayes factor.

section: Plotting standard error bars of point estimates
text:
Plotting standard error bars of point estimates
Now ready to plit the standard error bars of mean maths score by race as shown below.

ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x=RACE, 
        ymin=mean-se, 
        ymax=mean+se), 
    width=0.2, 
    colour="black", 
    alpha=0.9, 
    linewidth=0.5) +
  geom_point(aes
           (x=RACE, 
            y=mean), 
           stat="identity", 
           color="red",
           size = 1.5,
           alpha=1) +
  ggtitle("Standard error of mean maths score by race")














TipThings to learn from the code chunk




The error bars are computed using formula mean +/- se
For geom_point(), it is important to indicate stat=“identity”

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 3 - Visualising Uncertainty
section: Plotting confidence interval of point estimates
text:
Plotting confidence interval of point estimates
We can also plot confidence intervals of mean maths score by race.

ggplot(my_sum) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(x=reorder(RACE, -mean), 
        ymin=mean-1.96*se, 
        ymax=mean+1.96*se), 
    width=0.2, 
    colour="black", 
    alpha=0.9, 
    linewidth=0.5) +
  geom_point(aes
           (x=RACE, 
            y=mean), 
           stat="identity", 
           color="red",
           size = 1.5,
           alpha=1) +
  labs(x = "Maths score",
       title = "95% confidence interval of mean maths score by race")














TipThings to learn from code chunk




Confidence intervals are computed by using formula mean +/- 1.96*se
Error bars is sorted by using the average maths scores
labs() arguments of ggplot is used to change the x-axis label

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 3 - Visualising Uncertainty
section: Visualising the uncertainty of point estimates with interactive error bars
text:
Visualising the uncertainty of point estimates with interactive error bars

shared_df = SharedData$new(my_sum)

bscols(widths = c(4,8),
       ggplotly(ggplot(shared_df) +
                  geom_errorbar(aes(
                    x=reorder(RACE, -mean),
                    ymin=mean-2.58*se, 
                    ymax=mean+2.58*se), 
                    width=0.2, 
                    colour="black", 
                    alpha=0.9, 
                    size=0.5) +
                  geom_point(aes(
                    x=RACE, 
                    y=mean, 
                    text = paste(
                      "Race:", `RACE`,
                      "<br>N:", `n`,
                      "<br>Avg. Scores:", round(mean, digits = 2),
                      "<br>95% CI:[", 
                      round((mean-2.58*se), digits = 2), ",",
                      round((mean+2.58*se), digits = 2),"]")),
                    stat="identity", 
                    color="red", 
                    size = 1.5, 
                    alpha=1) + 
                  xlab("Race") + 
                  ylab("Average Scores") + 
                  theme_minimal() + 
                  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
                    angle = 45, vjust = 0.5, hjust=1)) +
                  ggtitle("99% Confidence interval of average /<br>maths scores by race"), 
                tooltip = "text"), 
       DT::datatable(shared_df, 
                     rownames = FALSE, 
                     class="compact", 
                     width="100%", 
                     options = list(pageLength = 10,
                                    scrollX=T), 
                     colnames = c("No. of pupils", 
                                  "Avg Scores",

         formatRound(columns=c('mean', 'sd', 'se'),

stat_point_interval() method

exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, 
             y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval() +
  labs(
    title = "Visualising confidence intervals of mean math score",
    subtitle = "Mean Point + Multiple-interval plot")














Note



stat_pointinerval() comes with many arguments, please read the syntax reference for more detail.
For example, the code chunk below have the following arguments added: - .width = 0.95 - .point = median - .interval = qi

exam %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = RACE, 
             y = MATHS)) +
  stat_pointinterval(.width = 0.95,
                     .point = median,
                     .interval = qi) +
  labs(
    title = "Visualising confidence intervals of median math score",
    subtitle = "Median Point + Multiple-interval plot")

text:
Basic plot

funnel_plot(
  .data = covid19,
  numerator = Positive,
  denominator = Death,
  group = `Sub-district`
)








A funnel plot object with 267 points of which 0 are outliers. 
Plot is adjusted for overdispersion. 








TipThings to learn from the code chunk




group argument here is different from scatterplot. Here, it defines the level of the points to be plotted (i.e. Sub-district, District, City). If City is chosen, there are only six data points.
By default data_type argument is “SR” (standard ratio)
limit accepted values 95 or 99 corresponding to 95% or 99.8% quantiles of the distribution

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 4 - Funnel Plots for Fair Comparisons
text:
Makeover 1
Lets change the numerator and denominator values so that the comparison is insteadlly the fatality rate (deaths per positive case). data_type is also changed to “PR” (proportion) which will give us the direct ratio and not scaled. And set range for x and y axis.

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 4 - Funnel Plots for Fair Comparisons
text:
Compute basic derived fields
To plot the funnel plot from scratch, we need to derive cumulative detah rate and standard error of cumulative death rate

df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death / Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate*(1-rate)) / (Positive))) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)

Next, the fit.mean is computed.

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1/df$rate.se^2)

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 4 - Funnel Plots for Fair Comparisons
section: Calculate lower and upper limits for 95% and 99.9% CI
text:
Calculate lower and upper limits for 95% and 99.9% CI

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
dfCI <- data.frame(number.ll95, number.ul95, number.ll999, 
                   number.ul999, number.seq, fit.mean)

title: Hands-on Exercise 4 Part 4 - Funnel Plots for Fair Comparisons
text:
Plot a static funnel plot

p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Positive, y = rate)) +
  geom_point(aes(label=`Sub-district`), 
             alpha=0.4) +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ll95), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40", 
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ul95), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40", 
            linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ll999), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(data = dfCI, 
            aes(x = number.seq, 
                y = number.ul999), 
            size = 0.4, 
            colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(data = dfCI, 
             aes(yintercept = fit.mean), 
             size = 0.4, 
             colour = "grey40") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim=c(0,0.05)) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = -0.13, label = "95%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  annotate("text", x = 4.5, y = -0.18, label = "99%", size = 3, colour = "grey40") + 
  ggtitle("Cumulative Fatality Rate by Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") +
  xlab("Cumulative Number of COVID-19 Cases") + 
  ylab("Cumulative Fatality Rate") +
  theme_light() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size=12),
        legend.position = c(0.91,0.85), 
        legend.title = element_text(size=7),
        legend.text = element_text(size=7),
        legend.background = element_rect(colour = "grey60", linetype = "dotted"),
        legend.key.height = unit(0.3, "cm"))
p
